extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and legal practitioners (19th-century British/ comparative US context)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and practical guidance for patent validity, property/assignment issues, infringement, remedies, evidence and procedures for obtaining or cancelling patents (UK-focused with comparative notes on US law).

rubrics_metrics.name: No retrospective addition of new matter in later specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A subsequent specification cannot operate retrospectively to enable the patentee to say he possessed or had discovered an invention at an earlier date if that matter did not in fact exist or was not known at the date of the first patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the later machine contains new matter wholly incapable of having been present in the first, the latter is not an improvement of the former but an addition of new matter which was not known at the date of the first patent; such new matter cannot be treated as part of the original representation or consideration of the earlier grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of patents should favor sustaining grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents ought not to be subjected to excessive critical acumen as if the object were to defeat rather than to sustain them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid over-critical constructions that defeat patents; interpretive approach should consider the intention to sustain valid grants rather than to find defeat by hyper-technical reading (principle stated by Lord Tenterden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of assignments and licences (number of persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions arise about the power of granting licences and assignments, for example whether licences to companies of more than five persons or grants for particular districts are valid under the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provisions (6 Geo. I. c.18 s.18) that purportedly void a patent where power becomes vested in more than five persons were construed to apply to assignments by act of the party but not to assignments by operation of law (e.g., bankruptcy). Practical uncertainties remain (e.g., regranting licences, district-limited grants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy — assignees take patent interest (operation of law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent pass to assignees of a bankrupt by operation of law; statutory forfeiture clauses tied to assignments by the party do not apply to transfers by operation of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts held that the clause voiding patents where the interest became vested in more than five persons applied only to assignments by act of the party, so assignees under a commission of bankrupt were not within that clause; the assignees therefore retained the interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortgage and lien validity despite number of creditors
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortgage of a patent to more than five persons (creditors) appears valid because creditors' interests are not proportional patent rights but claims for debt repayment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because creditors do not acquire a proportionate share of the patent right itself, a mortgage to multiple creditors should not trigger forfeiture under the statute intended to prevent multiple owners; practice suggests such mortgages are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trusts of patents and foreign inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be the subject of a trust for the benefit of British subjects and may be communicated by a foreigner, but questions exist as to secret trusts where the real inventor is an alien enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The point whether a British subject may take out a patent on secret trust for an alien enemy (with the patentee stating he received the invention from a foreigner) was doubted and not solemnly decided—caution advised in such arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: What amounts to an infringement — multifactor test
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining infringement is difficult and drawn from many circumstances: expert evidence, concurring/contradictory testimony, and the public use of a supposed invention (public use is the best criterion whether it is an improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges and juries, aided by witnesses (mechanics, chemists, etc.), can decide infringement; the use made of an invention by the public is a strong indicator. The courts may accept testimony from skilled witnesses to determine whether devices are the same in principle and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making alone is an infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual making of the patented article constitutes infringement even if the article has not been sold or used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terms of a patent often read 'without leave or licence make, &c.' — so making the article (demonstrated by possession or manufacturing) is sufficient infringement (Jones v. Pearce example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings and venue considerations in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue historically laid in Middlesex for certain patent suits; the general issue plea is common and procedural improvements are desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule forbidding change of venue is criticized as expensive and unfair where witnesses are remote. It would be advantageous to allow defendants to deliver notice of objections with the plea to save expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence: prior specifications must be produced where improvement claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent claims 'improvements' upon an earlier patented machine, the earlier specification must be given in evidence to determine what was known before and what is truly new in the later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without knowing the prior specification, one cannot say what the improvements are; sometimes infringement may be presumed from acts (e.g., sales) where the defendant refuses to reveal manufacturing details or factory evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for challenging patents post-trial (rules on affidavits)
rubrics_metrics.description: On motions for a new trial, courts will not generally grant relief based solely on affidavits alleging prior knowledge; if facts disclosed would vitiate a patent, a scire facias is the proper remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit evidence on motion for new trial is contrary to practice; substantial allegations of invalidity should be pursued by scire facias rather than by overturning jury verdicts on affidavit alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs — experiments and scientific witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs of expensive experiments and fees for scientific witnesses in patent actions are treated under general rules, with limits on recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have directed that no allowance should be made for the expense of experiments, nor for the time of scientific witnesses unless they were medical men; trial courts review taxation of such items strictly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies: law vs equity and injunction practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings in equity are expensive and slow; common-law courts might be empowered to restrain infringers quickly; equity's main practical benefit is ordering the infringer to keep an account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court of Chancery rarely grants perpetual injunctions and commonly directs trial by feigned issue; an ability in common-law courts to grant interlocutory restraint/summons would be quicker and less costly, while accounts could be equally managed in common-law proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scire facias for repeal of patents — public action and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A scire facias is the process by which patents are declared void, but it is vexatious, expensive, and slow; it should be considered as an action by the public and unsuccessful challengers ought to bear costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative improvement is suggested; writ cannot be wholly superseded because the Crown should retain power to repeal improvident grants. Practical abuse: patentees may sue each other's patents out by scire facias, leading to mutual destruction of patents (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for declaring a patent void (novelty/prior use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are void if not new or if the invention had been used or known prior to the patent; statutory language about patents being 'contrary to the law nor mischievous to the state' is vague but potentially inoperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of prior use or prior description can vitiate a patent. The text criticizes alarmist statutory language but recognizes novelty and prior public use as core invalidating grounds (illustrated in cases where patents were mutually annulled).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence practice in scire facias (use of drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness may be asked to compare a drawing with a machine he made and may look at the drawing to judge whether it is a correct representation of his construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the drawing was not made by the witness, courts permit him to answer whether he recollects the machine sufficiently to state that the drawing is correct; demonstration and documentary comparison are admissible in establishing prior use or identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: US inventor eligibility and term
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States any citizen who has invented a new and useful art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or a new and useful improvement not known or used before the application, may be granted letters patent for up to fourteen years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor dies, legal representatives may obtain the patent. Aliens may obtain patents if they have resided two years in America and the invention has not been published abroad; Congress may pass special acts to relax these requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: US subject-matter requirement (what constitutes a 'manufacture')
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a US patent must be some new art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter; mere change of form or proportions does not constitute a discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements in principle or process may be patented, but mere changes in form/proportions are not discoveries. An improvement patent does not entitle the patentee to make/use the original invention without rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: US specification/enablement and disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The US schedule (specification) appended to letters patent must be a written description of the invention and the manner of using or the process of compounding it, in such full, clear, and exact terms as to distinguish it from all other things before known and to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For machines the inventor must explain the principle and the several contemplated modes of applying it, accompanied by drawings and written references where appropriate; for compositions supply specimens in sufficient quantity for experiment; a model must be delivered if the Secretary of State deems it necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: US practice to obtain patents (formal filing steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: The US practice involves payment of a fee, depositing a receipt and petition with a short title, making an oath/affirmation of inventorship (and residence if alien), filing a signed specification attested by two witnesses, and administrative examination/certification by the Attorney General and sealing/recording by the Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Attorney General must certify within fifteen days whether the patents conform to law; the specification must be signed and attested by two witnesses and filed in the Secretary's office; delivery of models and drawings as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: US caveat/interfering applications arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: Where interfering applications arise from two persons, they are submitted to three arbitrators: one chosen by each applicant and a third by the Secretary of State, whose award is final; if more than two applicants and they cannot agree, the Secretary appoints all three arbitrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arbitration procedure for competing applications is final, providing a practical administrative resolution of priority disputes in the US patent system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive approach of US courts — liberal construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The reports of decisions in the US Supreme Court indicate judges incline to put a liberal construction on letters patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing patent claims and specifications US courts historically favored a liberal interpretation, which may affect scope and enforcement.
